message.content:
### Quick Check – Is **VS Code** (`Code.exe`) Running?

On Windows you can use `tasklist` from either Command Prompt or PowerShell:

```cmd
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq Code.exe"
```

#### What it does  
* `/FI` applies a filter; `"IMAGENAME eq Code.exe"` tells `tasklist` to list only processes whose executable name matches *exactly* “Code.exe”.
* If VS Code is running, you'll see an entry similar to this:

| Image Name | PID   | Session Name | Session # | Mem Usage |
|------------|-------|--------------|-----------|----------|
| Code.exe   | 12345 | Console      |        1 |  150,000 K |

If nothing appears under **Image Name**, then no instance of `Code.exe` is currently active.

---

## Using It Inside a Batch File

If you want to automate a decision based on whether VS Code is open, wrap the call in a simple `.bat` file:

```batch
@echo off
rem --- Check for Code.exe ------------------------------------
for /f "tokens=2 delims==," %%i in ('tasklist ^| findstr /I "Code.exe"') do (
    set CODE_PID=%%i
)

if defined CODE_PID (
    echo VS Code is running (PID %CODE_PID%).
) else (
    echo VS Code is NOT running.
)
pause
```

> **Tip:** In scripts you often prefer `findstr /R "^Code\.exe$"` so you avoid matching other names containing “code”.

---

## Alternative: PowerShell

PowerShell offers a more idiomatic way:

```powershell
Get-Process -Name Code -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

or simply test existence:

```powershell
if (Get-Process -Name Code -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    Write-Host "VS Code is running."
}
else {
    Write-Host "VS Code is NOT running."
}
```

This returns the process object when found, otherwise `$null`.

---

## Common Pitfalls & Gotchas

| Issue | Fix/Note |
|------|---------|
| **Case sensitivity** | `tasklist` filters case‑insensitively, but always match exactly (“Code.exe”). |
| **Multiple instances** | If several windows/tabs are opened, each may spawn its own `Code.exe`. All will appear as separate rows. |
| **Admin rights** | You don’t usually need elevated permissions just to read the process table. |
| **Hidden processes** | Some background services may hide themselves; `tasklist` shows all visible ones unless filtered out. |

---

### TL;DR

Run:

```cmd
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq Code.exe"
```

and look for a row named `Code.exe`. No such row → VS Code isn’t running. Yes → it’s up!
